summary: Explains how to produce DNSKEY and RRSIG records for DNSSEC using RSA with SHA-256 and SHA-512. These algorithms give DNSSEC stronger hash functions than SHA-1. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS answers can carry a signature to prove they are real. This document says how to make those signatures with stronger math that is harder for a cheater to fake.

questions: how to use sha-256 with rsa in dnssec
what key sizes does dnssec rsa sha-2 allow
why use sha-2 instead of sha-1 in dnssec
subtitle: How DNSSEC keys and signatures are made with RSA and the SHA-256 and SHA-512 hash functions.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC signatures at the time relied on RSA with SHA-1, and confidence in SHA-1 was being eroded by recently announced attacks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two algorithms, RSA/SHA-256 (number 8) and RSA/SHA-512 (number 10), and specifies how to store their DNSKEY data and build RRSIG signatures with the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 scheme.
tldr.outcome: DNSSEC users are encouraged to deploy SHA-2 as soon as software allows. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6944.

today: RFC 5702 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2009 and is updated by RFC 6944. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Adding SHA-2 to DNSSEC
sections.content:
DNSSEC extends the Domain Name System with cryptographic keys and digital signatures so the authenticity and integrity of DNS data can be verified. RFC 4034 describes how to store DNSKEY and RRSIG resource records and lists the algorithms to use.

This RFC extends that list with RSA/SHA-256 and RSA/SHA-512. It assumes the reader knows DNSSEC, RSA and the SHA-2 family. The name SHA-2 is used here only for SHA-256 and SHA-512, since SHA-224 and SHA-384 are not used in DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS has a list of ways to sign its answers. This document adds two stronger ways to the list.

sections.title: DNSKEY Records for RSA/SHA-2
sections.content:
RSA public keys for RSA/SHA-256 are stored in DNSKEY records with algorithm number 8. For RSA/SHA-512 the algorithm number is 10. The DNSKEY record format itself is the one in RFC 4034.

Key sizes are limited. RSA/SHA-256 keys MUST NOT be less than 512 bits and MUST NOT be more than 4096 bits. RSA/SHA-512 keys MUST NOT be less than 1024 bits and MUST NOT be more than 4096 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of signing gets a number badge, 8 or 10. Keys come in a limited range of sizes, like locks that cannot be too tiny or too huge.

sections.title: Building an RRSIG Signature
sections.content:
The signature field of an RRSIG record follows the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 scheme. First a hash is computed: hash = SHA-XXX(data), where XXX is 256 or 512 and data is the wire format of the signed resource record set.

The signature is then ( 00 | 01 | FF* | 00 | prefix | hash ) ** e (mod n), where e is the private exponent and n the public modulus. The FF octet MUST be repeated so the concatenated term is as long as the modulus.

The prefix is an ASN.1 DER algorithm designator taken from PKCS #1 v2.1 (RFC 3447) to make standard cryptographic libraries easier to use. RSA/SHA-256 signatures use algorithm number 8 and a prefix ending in 04 20. RSA/SHA-512 signatures use algorithm number 10 and a prefix ending in 04 40.
sections.plainLanguage: To sign, you first squash the message into a short fingerprint, then wrap the fingerprint in a standard envelope and lock it with your secret key.

sections.title: Deployment and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
Apart from the minimum and maximum sizes, the RFC does not say what key size to use; that is an operational issue, and it points to NIST SP 800-57. Signature size depends on the key length, not the hash, so RSA/SHA-256 or RSA/SHA-512 RRSIG records are the same size as RSA/SHA-1 ones when the keys have the same length.

DNSSEC-aware implementations SHOULD support records created with these algorithms. The RFC does not define algorithm aliases of the kind RFC 5155 used to signal NSEC3 support. A validator implementing RSA/SHA-2 MUST be able to validate negative answers using both NSEC and NSEC3 with hash algorithm 1. An authoritative server without NSEC3 MAY still serve RSA/SHA-2 zones using NSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: The new seals are no bigger than the old ones if the key is the same size. Anyone who checks seals should know how to check both of the ways DNS says an answer does not exist.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives a complete key and signature for each algorithm. In both, an RRset of one A record, www.example.net. 3600 IN A 192.0.2.91, is signed with a zone signing key, with an inception of 00:00 on January 1st, 2000 and an expiration of 00:00 on January 1st, 2030.

The RSA/SHA-256 example uses algorithm 8 and key tag 9033 with a 512-bit key. The RSA/SHA-512 example uses algorithm 10 and key tag 3740 with a 1024-bit key. Implementers can use them as test vectors.
sections.plainLanguage: The document shows two finished examples so you can check that your own sealing machine gives the same result.

sections.title: IANA Registry Entries
sections.content: The RFC adds two entries to the IANA registry of DNS security algorithm numbers. Value 8 is RSA/SHA-256 (mnemonic RSASHA256) and value 10 is RSA/SHA-512 (mnemonic RSASHA512). Both are marked for zone signing. There has been no determination of standardization of the use of these algorithms with transaction security.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number list now has two new lines, 8 and 10, one for each new kind of seal.

sections.title: Why SHA-2 and Downgrade Resistance
sections.content:
DNSSEC users are encouraged to deploy SHA-2 as soon as software allows. SHA-2 is widely believed to be more resilient to attack than SHA-1, and confidence in SHA-1 is being eroded by recently announced attacks. SHA-2 is considered sufficiently strong for the immediate future. The RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 scheme was chosen to match the one used for RSA/SHA-1 so implementation is easier.

Each RRset MUST be signed with each algorithm present in the DNSKEY RRset at the zone apex (RFC 4035). A malicious party therefore cannot strip the RSA/SHA-2 signature to force the validator onto the RSA/SHA-1 one, which gives resilience against algorithm downgrade attacks if the validator supports RSA/SHA-2.
sections.plainLanguage: If a zone shows both an old and a new seal, a cheater cannot hide the new one to trick you into trusting only the old, weaker one.
